<pre style='white-space:pre-wrap;width:81ex'>feat(flat-history): windowed and per-address archive on the flat database (#12943)

* feat(history): rolling window groundwork

Scoped availability floors, bounded scan+delete pruner with scope
drain, config-gated changeset sidecar, and the transport-agnostic
import seam for the windowed archive program.

* feat(history): v3 pre-value window format

Deferred-fill capture with persisted-flat fallback reads, capped
self-destruct pre-value materialization with poison markers,
sidecar chunk splitting, and markers-only pivot seeding.

* feat(network): nhist/1 history serving protocol

Serves windowed history and block changesets to peers: range and
changeset requests with cursor continuation, served-scope handshake,
per-peer quotas, and snap-discipline response caps.

* feat(history): peer-fed window backfill importer

Key-sharded pre-sorted bulk import below the sync anchor with inline
per-block digest verification, bounded bisect-and-refetch recovery,
evidence-based connected-range publication, and prune interlock.

* fix(test): adapt importer tests to the v3 reader signature

* fix(history): cross-lane review fixes for the window program

Single row-format owner across writer, reader, pruner, server and
importer; pre-values on the changeset wire; sidecar capture on the
persisted tier, retention and byte-cap eviction, record-boundary
chunking; shared availability with CAS floors and scope draining;
nhist quota, disposal and rate-window fixes; async backfill gate.

* feat(history): per-contract slice scopes

Point-scope availability records with reconcile-on-startup config,
scope-aware pruning across all window columns, restricted read
bundles serving sliced addresses below the general floor, and a
budgeted union-merge for as-of range serving with gate and skew
protection.

* feat(history): sliced receipt retention and serving polish

Receipts for blocks matching sliced addresses are rewritten
self-describing and retained through pruning so eth_getLogs answers
from retained receipts; served-scope caching off the network thread.

* feat(history): full archive clone via the serving protocol

Raw row streaming with cursor continuation and per-column selection,
a clone importer over the sharded bulk-write pipeline with metadata
progress and destination-synced durability, marker-anchored
verification with ban-on-resolved-mismatch, and fail-closed refusals
for windowed sources, cancellations and format mismatches.

* feat(history): devp2p client glue for the window and clone feeds

Concrete nhist import sources with paging and refusal propagation,
handshake-driven peer selection, a peer sink wired to disconnects,
and config-gated coordinators for backfill and clone runs.

* fix(network): advertise nhist for history consumers

The capability only activates when both hellos carry it, so clone
and windowed-backfill clients must advertise it too, not only
serving nodes.

* perf(flat-history): make the archive clone fast, observable and failure-proof

- serve GetHistoryRows scans with readahead instead of cache-miss-only hints
- clone with concurrent shard streams (default 2, capped under the nhist in-flight limit)
- dedicated request sizer for row pages (512KB floor) off the snap sizer
- progress logging every 30s with rows/bytes/rate and per-column completion
- per-column done markers + stored target watermark: resume never re-clones finished columns and never publishes coverage the rows do not have
- refused pages retry with backoff; stream timeouts retry instead of silently abandoning the clone
- nhist serve requests get an 8s scheduler budget; served-bytes throttle sleeps only the window remainder off the deadline token
- Sync.HistoryServingMaxBytesPerSecond replaces the hardcoded 8MB/s serving cap
- clone + windowed retention is now an explicit startup configuration error
- thread-safe request id source (Random.Shared)

* feat(flat-history): clone source eligibility diagnostics and shared in-flight limit

- the clone coordinator logs once a minute WHY each connected nhist peer is not an eligible source (no satellite / SupportsFullClone=false / row format mismatch)
- per-peer in-flight limit moved to IHistoryServer and shared by the handler and the importer clamp
- document the 1MiB serving cap floor; completion log states bytes fetched this run

* fix(network): bind satellite protocols to their own session's sync peer

With mutual static peers both sides dial simultaneously, producing two
sessions of which duplicate resolution kills one. Satellite registration
looked the sync peer up in the pool BY NODE, so a satellite initialized on
the surviving session could bind to the dying session's sync peer (and
vice versa), leaving the surviving peer with no satellite protocol at all.
nhist made this visible - the archive clone selector permanently skipped
an eligible feeder with 'no nhist satellite protocol registered' - but any
satellite (snap included) can be stranded the same way on simultaneous
dials. Registration and the parked-handler flush now match strictly on
SessionId. Also: nhist status exchange and satellite registration now log
at Info, so source eligibility is diagnosable from default logs.

* feat(network): reserved serving slots for inbound nhist peers

A full serving node rejected history consumers dialing in - the general
peer pool fills and the post-Hello capacity shed cut them off, forcing
operators to pre-register every consumer as a static peer on the server,
backwards for a publish-only feeder. Inbound peers that advertise nhist
are now kept past MaxActivePeers in a dedicated budget
(Network.NHistServingPeerSlots, default 8) when this node advertises
nhist itself, so consumers connect with zero pre-arrangement.

* fix(network): make satellite registration resilient to session races

A satellite could still miss its sync peer: when eth had already completed
on a different session of the same node, the strict same-session binding
parked the satellite forever, and the parked-handler flush only accepted
same-session entries. Registration now goes to both the session's own
sync peer and the node's pooled sync peer, the handler is always parked
so a later eth completion picks it up, and the flush registers every
parked handler whose session is still alive (dead sessions are already
pruned on disconnect).

* fix(network): nhist handler self-registers on the sync peer pool with retries

The ProtocolsManager parking/flush bookkeeping still missed the satellite
registration for the one peer that matters under tight session timing, so
the clone selector kept seeing an initialized sync peer without an nhist
satellite. The handler now registers itself: after the status exchange it
polls the sync peer pool (2s interval, 2min budget) and registers on the
pooled sync peer as soon as it exists - the same object the selector
reads - making registration independent of protocol/session event
ordering. The manager-side paths stay as redundant idempotent writers.

* fix(network): register satellites from the session's own handlers at sync peer creation

Replaces the polling self-registration with the deterministic source of
truth: when a session's eth sync peer completes, any satellite protocol
already initialized on that same session (snap, nhist) is registered
directly from the session's protocol handler table. No dictionaries, no
event ordering, no cross-session ambiguity: the session object cannot
disagree with itself about which handlers it carries. Satellites that
initialize after eth completion keep the existing same-session direct
path; the parked-handler machinery remains as a redundant fallback.

* refactor(network): single deterministic satellite registration and honest serving-slot gate

Satellite registration is now exactly two same-session paths: at eth sync
peer creation the session's own initialized handlers register (primary),
and a satellite initializing after eth registers via the session's sync
peer directly; the cross-session pool registration is gone and parking is
back to a fallback for the not-yet-completed case only. The serving-slot
eligibility now asks the real question - does this node advertise history
serving (shared NHistP2PCapabilityResolver.AdvertisesServing) - instead
of 'does it advertise nhist at all', so consumer-only nodes no longer
grant serving slots.

* feat(config): mainnet_archive_clone profile

One-flag bootstrap for a full archive cloned from an existing serving
node: snap sync for the head, nhist/1 clone for flat history, and full
bodies/receipts download to genesis (the mainnet_archive profile
deliberately disables both download flags for replay archives, which
silently starves a fast-synced clone of its historical blocks). Shares
mainnet_archive's database path so a completed clone can be operated as
a plain archive node afterwards. The operator adds only the feeder's
enode via Network.StaticPeers.

* refactor(network): session-keyed satellite parking and self-contained serving slots

Applies the review findings on today's peering changes:
- the satellite parking dictionary is keyed by SessionId, making the
  eth-completion flush strictly same-session, turning disconnect cleanup
  into one TryRemove, and closing the per-node entry leak; the session
  handler-list registration and its hardcoded protocol list are gone
- PeerManager answers slot eligibility itself via the session's agreed
  capabilities and ISyncConfig (serving explicitly on, inbound only,
  dedup, removed on disconnect) - IPeerManager and ProtocolsManager are
  back to their upstream shapes
- the reserved slots raise the pre-Hello admission ceiling so they no
  longer consume the general margin; the knob moves to
  Sync.HistoryServingPeerSlots next to the other serving settings
- the nhist peer status publishes as one immutable snapshot, so a
  concurrent selector read can no longer observe a torn status
- the satellite registry on sync peers is a ConcurrentDictionary,
  removing a remote-triggerable dictionary race
- nhist-specific Info logging left only in the nhist handler

* fix(network): 30s response timeout for nhist row pages

Bulk row pages were cut by the general 10s response timeout whenever the
feeder was momentarily busy (serving snap and the clone to the same peer
while processing blocks), and each cut restarted the whole column stream
from its cursors - progress survived but the stream churned. Row-page
requests are a bulk transfer, not gossip: they now wait up to 30s, above
the server's 8s serve budget plus queueing and transfer, so a slow page
completes instead of tearing the stream down. The response-timeout
plumbing gains an optional per-request timeout, defaulting to the
existing 10s everywhere else.

* fix(flat-history): retry clone pages on timeout instead of tearing the stream down

The live feeder exhibits the known process-wide pauses of the flat
archive (tens of seconds, all serving frozen - bodies and nhist alike),
so any single page can exceed the response timeout even at 30s. A timed
out page now retries in place, same as a refused one, riding out a
paused source for up to the retry budget; only a persistently dead
source still surfaces to the coordinator's reconnect path.

* fix(nhist): answer dropped serves with Refused and recycle sessions that keep timing out

A GetHistoryRows serve that does not fit in the background task queue was
dropped without any response, leaving the requesting peer waiting for the
full response timeout while the serving node looked healthy. The server now
sends a Refused rows response for the request id it could not schedule, so
the client backs off and retries instead of stalling.

On the client side, three consecutive row response timeouts on the same
session now disconnect it, so the static-peer redial replaces a wedged
transport with a fresh session instead of retrying into a black hole.

* fix(network): dial disconnected static peers even when the peer pool is full

Outgoing dials are slot-gated end to end: the update iteration, candidate
selection and candidate queueing all bail out when no active peer slot is
free. Static peers are exempt from the capacity caps once connected, but a
disconnected static peer was never redialed while the pool sat at its
maximum, which starves it forever on a node whose pool stays saturated.

The update loop now redials any static peer that has no open session before
the slot gate, pacing retries with the existing connection-delay stats and
clearing a stale active-peer entry first so the fresh session can attach.

* fix(nhist): refuse over-quota row requests and count cancelled requests as timeouts

When the serving node stalls, its in-flight quota stays occupied by the
stuck serves, so the retrying consumer's next page request breached the
quota and the server tore the whole session down. Row requests over the
quota now get a Refused response, which the consumer already answers with
a short back-off, so a stall degrades into a polite retry loop instead of
a disconnect.

On the consumer side a request that dies without a response surfaces
either as TimeoutException or as a cancellation depending on which
timeout path wins the race; the cancellation shape bypassed both the page
retry and the consecutive-timeout session recycling, leaving a dead
session pinned as connected for hours. Both shapes now count as timeouts.

* feat(flat-history): detached capture bridges the archive clone to the tip

A clone client's own capture used to disable itself permanently on its
first persist: the walk cannot connect to genesis (the blocks below the
snap pivot were never processed locally), so every block processed while
the clone backfilled was lost and the node could never serve the range
between the clone watermark and its own head.

With HistoryArchiveCloneEnabled, an unconnected capture walk now records
into a durable pending range [first, last] instead of disabling: rows and
per-block markers are written as usual, each persist extends the range,
and nothing in it is served (reads above the watermark stay refused, fail
closed). When the clone completes and publishes its watermark W, the next
capture walk that connects to the pending range with first <= W + 1
publishes the watermark all the way to the persisted head in one step -
the union is contiguous from genesis - and clears the pending range;
capture then advances the watermark normally and the source feeder is no
longer needed. A watermark short of the range's bottom leaves the hole
unserved and logs what to do, never bridging silently.

The end state for a single-config clone node: snap sync to the tip, clone
[genesis, W] from the feeder, own capture [pivot, tip] recorded in
parallel, merged into one contiguous archive from genesis to the tip that
keeps advancing on its own.

* fix(network): a fresh inbound session from the same node replaces its stale open one

When a peer's session dies without the FIN ever reaching us (the remote
crashed mid-serve, or tore the connection down while stalled), our half
stays open and every reconnect attempt from that peer was rejected with
SessionAlreadyExist against a session the remote will never speak on
again - the peer stayed unreachable until one of the processes restarted.

An inbound session is RLPx-authenticated, so a fresh dial from the same
node id is proof the dialer considers its previous session dead. The
same-direction conflict now keeps the new inbound session and sheds the
stale one instead of the reverse. Outbound duplicates keep first-wins:
both dials are ours and the existing session has no staleness signal.

* fix(flat-history): re-clone until the cloned watermark reaches the node's own capture

The clone freezes its target watermark when it starts, but the snap pivot
keeps re-pivoting toward the head for as long as state sync runs, so on a
fresh node the pivot always lands hours of blocks above the frozen
watermark - a guaranteed gap between the cloned history and the node's own
capture that the fail-closed merge correctly refuses to bridge, leaving
every read above the watermark refused forever.

The coordinator now waits after a completed pass: if the capture connects
(watermark advances past the clone target), the archive is contiguous from
genesis to the tip and the loop ends; if the pending capture range starts
above the target instead, the pass state (stored watermark, done markers,
shard cursors) is reset and the clone re-runs against the source's current
watermark. The capture start is fixed once sync lands while the source
watermark grows with time, so the gap closes and the loop terminates.

* fix(network): scope inbound session replacement to nhist sessions only

Replacing any same-id inbound session proved too broad: it changed session
lifetime for every peer on the network and disturbed sync-peer allocation
(snap range downloads starved on a fresh sync). Only the clone pair
actually needs new-session-wins - a consumer that locally shed a dead
session and immediately redials - so the replacement now applies only when
the existing session has the nhist capability agreed. Every other peer
keeps the upstream first-wins duplicate rule, byte for byte.

* fix(snap): stop a flat node from poisoning snap sync, and rotate off a peer that keeps failing

A flat node advertised snap serving by default, but its root index promises
the last N roots from the block tree while the in-memory tier can only
materialize the ones compaction has not merged away - most requests answer
empty (or burn scheduler workers in gather retries, starving nhist serving
alongside). Flat nodes now default SnapServingEnabled off, in both places
that race to default it; an operator can still opt in explicitly.

On the consuming side, the stale-pivot heuristic wiped the failure log
after every pivot update, so a peer that stays the allocator's favorite
while never delivering could never accumulate enough failures to be
punished - snap starved forever on one poisonous fast peer. A second
failure streak with no success since the last pivot update now punishes
the peer so allocation rotates to the healthy ones.

Also debounces the static-peer redial queueing, which could double-queue
the same peer in back-to-back update iterations at startup.

* fix(flat-history): report the clone gap once per watermark instead of every persist

The genesis seed publishes watermark 0 at boot, so a fresh clone node hit
the gap report on every single capture walk for the whole duration of the
first clone pass - an Error-level line every persist saying to wipe and
re-clone, which is no longer even the right advice now that the
coordinator re-clones on its own. Downgraded to Info, deduplicated to one
report per distinct imported watermark, and reworded to describe the
transient state instead of prescribing a manual recovery.

* tune(nhist): tolerate a serving node's persist window before recycling the session

Live observation: a busy archive source starves its serving reads for up
to a minute on every flat persist cycle while its block processing runs
uninterrupted. Three consecutive row timeouts (~50s) tripped just under
that window, so the consumer recycled the session on every flush of the
source and paid a redial round-trip each time. Five strikes outlast the
window; a genuinely dead transport still gets recycled, just one retry
later.

* fix(network): name why a static peer is not being redialed, and fire the strike disconnect once

A static peer stayed unredialed for 10+ minutes after its session died and
nothing at Info level said why - the skip reasons (dial in flight,
reconnection delay) were invisible. Each skip reason now logs once per
minute so a stuck redial names its cause immediately; the absence of any
skip line while the peer stays disconnected points to a phantom open
session by elimination.

The consecutive-timeout disconnect also fired on every timeout past the
threshold, spamming the log and re-disconnecting a dead session - it now
fires exactly once per streak.

* fix(network): disconnect sessions that stop answering pings

A session whose transport dies without a FIN stays Initialized forever
because SessionMonitor only logs missed pongs. PeerManager then treats
the dead session as open and never redials the peer, which permanently
stalls static-peer connections. Disconnect after three consecutive
missed pongs, surface a stale-pong warning when a static peer is
skipped over such a session, and reject hello messages carrying this
node's own identity so hairpinned self-connections no longer occupy
peer slots.

* fix(flat-history): close the remaining archive clone operational gaps

Never dial our own enode: discovery can hand a node its own record back
and a hairpinned NAT completes the loop, so candidate selection now
drops candidates carrying the local identity. Archive clone source
diagnostics aggregate peers without the nhist satellite into a single
line instead of dumping every connected peer once a minute. Enabling
Flat.HistoryArchiveCloneEnabled on a fast-syncing node now also turns
on historical bodies and receipts download to genesis, so one flag
yields a complete gap-free archive without per-network config edits.

* feat(flat-history): clone progress bar and persist-window patience

A refusing source is signalling live backpressure (its serving pauses
while it persists), so refusals now get their own retry budget that
outlasts any persist window instead of sharing the five-attempt timeout
budget and tearing the stream down mid-pause. The periodic clone log
now renders the same progress meter as the body and receipt downloads,
estimating column progress from each shard cursor's position in the
uniformly distributed key space.

* fix(network): keep the static flag when the peer is already pooled

NodesLoader loads the persisted peers db before the configured static
peers, and PeerPool.GetOrAdd keyed by node id lets the first arrival
win - so a static peer that is also in the peers db (any node that has
run for more than one session) silently loses its static status for the
whole session. StaticPeers enumerates empty, the static redial loop
guards nothing, and after a mid-run disconnect the peer is only ever
redialed if a general peer slot happens to be free. Promote the static,
trusted, and bootnode flags onto the pooled instance instead of
dropping them. Also read the session fields once in the static-peer
check so a concurrent disconnect cannot null them between the check and
the use.

* fix(network): disconnect sessions that stop answering pings

A session whose transport dies without a FIN stays Initialized forever:
SessionMonitor only logs a missed pong and moves on, so the zombie
keeps its peer slot and, because same-direction session conflicts are
resolved first-wins, the peer cannot reconnect until the process
restarts. Disconnect after three consecutive missed pongs; any pong
resets the counter. The pre-existing (Explicit) Will_keep_pinging test
already expected the unresponsive session to end Disconnected.

* review: derive the tolerance from LastPongUtc, log at debug

LastPongUtc is initialised at construction and only ever advanced by a
received pong, so the pong age carries the same three-strike signal as
a side counter without the extra lifetime to keep in sync with
RemoveSession or its re-insertion leak window. The disconnect log drops
to debug: a peer dying without a FIN is routine churn, and the session
already logs the disconnect itself. Tests now pin the tolerance (a
session that recovers between missed pongs stays open) and the
disconnect reason, which selects the reconnect delay and lets the
privileged-node gate reap dead static sessions.

* review: name the constant after the window it defines, pin the tolerance

The check is a time window measured from the last pong, not a miss
counter, and the reap therefore lands on the fourth missed ping rather
than the third - the name now says intervals and states the effective
window. The tolerance test drives two consecutive misses before a pong,
so it fails if the window is narrowed, with a longer interval to keep
scheduler jitter well inside the margin.

* fix(flat-history): refuse a resume source that covers less than the frozen target

A clone pass freezes its target watermark on first start and keeps
streaming against it after an interruption, including when it resumes
from a different peer. Source selection checked full-clone support and
the row format but not coverage, so a replacement peer whose own
history ends below the frozen target would serve what it has, leave the
rows above its watermark unfetched, and the pass would still publish
the frozen target as covered - a silent hole at the top of the range.
Carry the stored target into peer selection and skip a peer that cannot
reach it, naming the shortfall in the diagnostics. Selection is
unconstrained when no pass is in progress, so a first clone and the
post-reset re-clone are unaffected.

* review: drop the redundant disconnect log

The missed pong is already logged a few lines up and the session logs
the disconnect with its reason and details, so the line in between only
repeated them.

* feat(flat-history): advertise history serving in the ENR and verify a clone before publishing it

A consumer could only reach a server that was configured as a static
peer: the capability is negotiated after a connection exists, so there
was no way to find one. Serving nodes now carry an nhist entry in their
own record - format version and whether they serve a full archive, the
facts a consumer needs to reject a server before spending a dial, and
stable enough not to force a re-sign - contributed through a hook so
the record provider stays unaware of history. Discovered servers are
dialed under their own small budget, sized to the shards a peer can
carry at once, rather than competing with block, body and receipt sync
for general peer slots.

Publishing a cloned range is now gated on its state roots agreeing with
the headers this node synced independently. The source chose the rows
it served but had no say in those headers, so a fabricated or shifted
root index cannot satisfy both; an unchecked range would otherwise be
answered from and served onward, since a node that finishes a clone
becomes a server itself.

* fix(flat-history): reject forged code, keep the watermark monotonic, unwind two serving hazards

Code rows were written verbatim into the node's live code database, and
code is read back by hash without ever being re-hashed, so a clone
source could put bytecode of its choosing behind a hash the EVM
executes. Every imported code row is now required to hash to its own
key, which needs no peer, header or consensus input to decide.

Publishing a watermark could lower it. A completed clone keeps its
stored target on disk, so a restart re-ran the pass, skipped every
finished column and republished that target - by then far below the
head the node had been capturing - un-covering everything in between
and leaving the coordinator waiting for a connection that could never
happen, re-streaming the archive on every restart. Publishing is now
monotonic.

The serving-slot list was taken before the session lock, while a
session conflict holds that lock across a synchronous disconnect that
wants the list: two threads tearing down sessions could deadlock all
peer management. It is now guarded by the session lock like every other
session-lifetime collection here.

The byte throttle slept inside a shared background executor with an
uncancellable delay, so a consumer at full rate could park capacity
that every subprotocol's serving needs and hold it through block
processing. An over-budget peer is now refused before the scan runs,
and the remaining wait honours the caller's token.

* fix(nhist): keep served scans out of the block cache and close an iterator leak

A served history scan walked both the history column and, when it needs the
flat fallback, the same account column block processing reads from. Both
iterators ran with default read flags, so every page a peer asked for filled
the shared block cache with rows this node will never read again, evicting its
own hot state to answer someone else. Both views now scan with HintCacheMiss
so the pages stay out of the cache, keeping HintReadAhead for the sequential
walk itself.

The flat view was also acquired before the history view entered its try block:
if opening the second iterator threw, the first one leaked its native handle
and pinned the SST files it held open until the process exited. The flat view
is now opened inside the try that disposes it.

* fix(nhist): reserve history source slots only on a node that imports history

Sync.HistorySourcePeerSlots defaulted to 6 on every node, so any node at all
kept six outbound connection slots, above the general peer limit, for peers
advertising nhist serving. That advertisement is a self-declared ENR entry
anyone can publish, which made it a lever for steering extra connections onto
nodes that have no importer to use them.

The setting is now nullable and unset by default. FlatHistoryModule resolves
it at build time to the reservation only when this node actually imports
history - an archive clone, or a retention window it has to backfill - and to
zero otherwise, so the slots exist exactly where something consumes them. An
explicit value in config still wins over both.

* fix(nhist): let row requests keep their full timeout and drop stale debounce entries

Row requests are sent with a 30s response timeout, deliberately longer than
the default, because a serving node under a persist window can stall reads for
tens of seconds and recycling the session costs a redial. The dictionary
holding those requests was built with the default cleanup threshold of 15s, so
it removed the request and completed it with a TimeoutException well before
its own budget expired - and if the honest response then arrived, Handle threw
SubprotocolException for an unrequested response, disconnecting a peer that had
done nothing wrong. The rows dictionary now cleans up at 1.5x its request
timeout, the same ratio the default uses, so the request-level timeout is the
one that decides.

The three dial-debounce dictionaries also never removed anything. Static ones
are bounded by config, but the history-source one is keyed by any peer
publishing the nhist ENR entry, which is a self-declared entry and therefore
unbounded remote-driven growth against a peer pool that is itself bounded and
evicts. All three now drop their entry when the pool removes the peer.

* fix(nhist): refuse a clone whose range the root check cannot sample, and stop retuning the shared code db

The sampled-root gate compares imported state roots against headers this node
synced independently, and it skipped itself whenever the target watermark did
not rise above the local retention floor - the one input it cannot sample. A
source is free to advertise that watermark: it could then serve arbitrary rows
into every history column, have the gate pass by doing nothing, and leave those
rows on disk for a later honest pass to publish over. The empty range is now
refused up front, before a single row is streamed, and the gate itself throws
on it as well rather than returning quietly.

The importer also tuned whichever database a column resolves to. Four of them
are history columns it owns, but the code column is the node-wide code
database, which state sync tunes for its own run - so a clone finishing its
code column reset a setting mid-sync that belonged to someone else, and took
the tuning away again on the way out. Tuning is now applied only to the columns
the importer owns.

* fix(nhist): abandon a clone whose source cursor never advances

The shard page loop ended only on a null cursor or on filling the write batch,
and neither is reachable if the source keeps answering with an empty page and
the same cursor it was handed. The importer then requested that page forever:
no rows written, no error raised, no shard ever finished, with the write batch
held open the whole time. Nothing about that requires malice - a buggy server
reaches it too - and there was no bound to stop it.

A cursor is now required to move past the one it was sent, which an honest
server always satisfies because it emits at least one row before it stops
short. A cursor that does not advance is a protocol violation and abandons the
import.

* review: widen the pong window and credit late pongs

A ping only goes out on every other tick: LastPingUtc is stamped after the
tick that sent it, so the guard fails on the next one and the effective ping
period is two intervals, measured at 999ms against a 500ms interval. A window
of three intervals therefore tolerated two missed pongs, not three, so widen
it to six.

A pong arriving after Timeouts.P2PPing no longer completes the in-flight
source, and nothing else refreshed LastPongUtc, so a peer whose latency
exceeds the per-ping timeout had every ping counted as a miss and was
eventually reaped although it never stopped answering. Stamp the session when
the pong is handled.

The test session helper left RemoteHost and RemotePort unset, so Session.Node
threw inside InitiateDisconnect and the ping loop swallowed it, which made the
recovery test pass against any threshold. Set both, assert the third ping
actually returned a pong, and anchor the pong baseline before the monitor
starts so the disconnect test tells tolerance apart from an immediate drop.

* fix(nhist): stop the archive clone freezing a target its own capture has outrun

A clone freezes its target watermark from the source it picks, and the pass is
only useful if that target meets the block where this node's own capture
starts. Nothing enforced that. In the mainnet run the capture start was already
recorded when the pass began, the source chosen sat 387 blocks below it, and
the two ranges could never touch - so 543 GB of StorageHistory streamed for
three hours, was declared complete, and was then re-fetched from scratch
against a fresh target. Roughly a third of every byte the clone moved was spent
on a pass that was doomed before its first request.

The peer selector already accepts a minimum watermark; it was only ever given
the resume target, which is zero on a fresh pass. It now also gets the recorded
capture start, so a source that cannot reach it is not eligible and the loop
waits for one that can, which costs seconds because the source advances every
block.

A capture that starts after the target was frozen can still strand a pass, so
the importer re-checks at each column boundary and abandons the pass there
instead of streaming columns whose rows it already knows will be discarded. The
coordinator drops the stored target on that path, otherwise the retry would
resume the same doomed one.

* perf(nhist): send a row key as a delta against the previous row

History keys are [flat key | block], so every version of a key repeats the flat
key verbatim. Measured on the mainnet archive: a storage row is 60 key bytes of
which 52 repeat, against an average value of 12 bytes, so the wire is mostly the
same key over and over. The clone moved 1.15 TB to build a 429 GB column, and
the on-disk figures show RocksDB storing the same rows in a third of that -
most of the difference is key repetition it delta-encodes and we do not.

Each entry now carries how many leading bytes it shares with the previous
entry's key instead of those bytes. Measured over 5 million real rows per
column, that is 29.0% off AccountHistory and 48.3% off StorageHistory, about
450 GB off a full clone.

This is confined to the serializer: entries still hold whole keys in memory, so
the server scan, the importer and the cursor logic are untouched.

* fix(nhist): a served scan that runs out of time returns what it has instead of refusing

A row scan that hit its cancellation checked the token, disposed everything it
had gathered, and answered Refused. The requester comes back with the same
cursor, so the server repeats the same scan and hits the same wall: a page that
cannot be finished once cannot be finished on a retry either. On a node busy
enough to cancel the scan at all, that is a livelock, and it is what filled the
clone's log with refusals while the source was otherwise healthy.

The scan now stops the same way it stops for its byte and entry caps: it keeps
the rows it gathered and hands back the cursor to resume from. Progress is
monotonic at any speed - a loaded server returns short pages instead of no
pages. Refusing is kept for the one case where it is the honest answer, a scan
cancelled before it gathered anything, since there is no cursor to hand back
that would move the requester on and echoing the one it sent would stall it.

Scanned entries are now bounded too, not just emitted ones. Rows dropped for a
wrong key length cost scan time without counting against any cap, so a range
holding many of them could run long with nothing to show; the cursor also now
advances past them rather than sending the next scan back over the same keys.

* test(nhist): pin that the code column is servable inside the importer's shard bounds

The archive clone reports the code column complete with zero rows against a
source holding 2.68 million of them, so this asserts the contract the clone
relies on: a 32-byte code hash inside shard 0's range streams out for the exact
one-byte start and MaxRowKeyBytes-long end the importer sends.

It passes, which is the point of recording it - the serving path is not where
the rows are lost, so the next place to look is narrower.

* diag(nhist): surface an empty served page and an empty cloned column

The clone reported the code column complete with zero rows against a source
holding 2.68 million of them, marked the column done, and moved on without a
word. Every later pass then skips it, so a momentary fault becomes a permanent
hole in a node that believes it holds a full archive.

Two places now say so. The importer warns when a column finishes having fetched
nothing, naming the consequence rather than leaving the operator to infer it
from a row count of zero in an info line. It stays a warning rather than a
failure because an empty column is legitimate for some sources and the importer
cannot tell the two apart from its side.

The server logs the column, the bounds it was given, the cursor it was handed
and the one it returned whenever it serves an empty page that it did not
refuse. Reading the code has not explained how a scan of a populated database
inside the shard's key range comes back empty, so the next step is to have the
server report what it actually saw.

* diag(nhist): report a serve the requester has already abandoned

The feeder's log is silent through every one of these stalls: no disconnect, no
quota breach, no missed pong, just the consumer reconnecting on a fresh port
every three minutes. Three minutes is five row timeouts of thirty seconds plus
the redial, so the consumer is the one giving up while the source never notices
anything is wrong - which means the interesting event is on the serving side
and currently leaves no trace.

Two lines close that. One when a serve cannot be scheduled at all, which is
answered with a refusal the operator otherwise only infers from the consumer's
side. One when a scan runs past its deadline, with how long it actually took,
since a scan that overruns is invisible today: the requester has already timed
out and the response goes nowhere.

* fix(nhist): stop a scan before the scheduler abandons it, so an answer always goes back

This is the cause of the three-minute stall cycle. The scheduler runs a serve
under an eight second deadline and, once it expires, drops the work without
sending anything. This morning's change made a cancelled scan return the rows
it had gathered, but cancellation is exactly the moment the scheduler has
already given up, so that response went nowhere. The requester waited its full
thirty seconds for silence, five times over, then recycled the session and
redialled - which is why the source logged nothing at all through every stall:
from its side a task was simply cancelled.

The scan now stops at five seconds of its own accord, leaving three to encode
and send whatever it has along with a cursor to resume from. A loaded source
answers with short pages instead of silence, and the requester keeps its
session.

Also guards the shard bounds the clone actually sends against the code
database's prefix-extractor configuration. A one-byte lower bound and a
128-byte upper bound sit in different capped:8 buckets, and a range scan that
respected the bucket rather than the bounds would silently return almost
nothing. It behaves correctly today; the test keeps a later options change from
breaking it in silence.

* fix(nhist): a column the source answered with nothing is not complete

The code column came back with zero rows against a source holding 2.68 million
of them, was marked done, and every pass since has skipped it. Whatever made
that first answer empty, treating it as complete is what turned a moment into a
permanent hole: the node now believes it holds a full archive and will serve one
to the next consumer.

An empty column no longer gets its done marker, so the next pass asks again. A
source that genuinely holds nothing there costs a handful of empty requests per
pass, which is the right price for not carrying a gap forward silently. The
warning names the situation either way.

* fix(nhist): ask for total order when opening a range view

The source's own log settled where the code rows go. It receives the request,
canServe is true, the bounds are exactly the shard's - start 00, end 0F followed
by FF - and the first key in its code database is 00000A69..., squarely inside
them. It then scans to exhaustion and returns nothing, with no continuation
cursor.

The code database is configured for point lookups: prefix_extractor capped:8, a
kHashSearch index and a prefix_hash memtable. On that shape an iterator is only
obliged to be correct inside the seek key's prefix bucket unless total order is
requested, so a range spanning buckets is free to come back empty - which is
what it does, while Get by hash keeps working and hides it.

A view promises every key between its bounds, so it now asks for total order.
Where no prefix extractor is configured, which is every history column, the
option changes nothing.

Noting honestly that the unit test written for this passes either way: sixteen
keys flush into a single data block where the hash index degenerates, so it
cannot reproduce what an 8 GB database across many levels does. It is kept to
guard the bounds shape, and the live run is what confirms the fix.

* fix(nhist): always answer a serve whose deadline expired while queued

The background scheduler sets a serve deadline when the request is enqueued, not
when it starts running, and hands an already-cancelled token to anything that
waited out its budget in the queue. The served-bytes throttle then took that
token into Task.Delay and threw, discarding a response that was already built -
including the refusal a saturated source needs to send. The requester saw
silence, paid a full 30s row timeout, and after five of those lost the session
and spent minutes redialling.

Cancellation now ends the throttle wait without propagating, so every accepted
request answers. The serve deadline moves to 20s so queue time no longer eats
the whole budget, while the real work stays bounded by the 5s scan deadline.

The clone-side log blamed these refusals on the source persisting; they are the
serving byte budget, and the wrong explanation cost days of looking elsewhere.

* refactor(nhist): stop sleeping a shared worker to rate-limit serving

The byte budget is already enforced where it belongs: an over-budget peer is
refused before its scan starts. Sleeping afterwards limited nothing, because the
work was done and the response built - it only parked one of a handful of shared
background executors and delayed a requester that could have been answered.

The window accounting stays, since that is what the pre-scan check reads. The
serve handlers that only awaited this sleep become synchronous.

* fix(flat-history): keep the detached capture floor from climbing every flush

The detached branch republished the pending capture range using the lowest block
of the current walk. That walk only reaches as far back as it can still lease
state, so after the first capture it starts higher, and each flush overwrote the
floor with a larger number. The other branch never had this problem: it carries
the stored floor forward.

A climbing floor eventually passes the frozen target of a running clone, which
makes the coordinator abandon the pass and clear every done marker and cursor -
so a clone that had already streamed hundreds of gigabytes started over, and
started over again on the next flush. It could not converge while the node was
still capturing.

The floor now only ever moves down, which is the only direction a lowest-block
can honestly move.

Raising a target also cannot stale content addressed by its hash, so the reset
leaves the code column alone rather than refetching every byte of code the node
already holds to arrive at identical rows.

* revert(flat-history): restore the detached capture floor to the current walk

The previous commit kept the stored floor when a walk could not reach the
pending range. That branch only runs when the two runs are discontiguous, so
carrying the old floor forward publishes a range spanning blocks this node never
captured, and as-of reads inside the hole would be served as covered.

Publishing the current walk's lowest block is correct: a pending range describes
one contiguous run, and an interrupted capture legitimately starts a new one.

Why the floor climbed on the feeder is therefore still open - the question is
what made its capture discontiguous, not this line.

* fix(archive-clone): wait for the capture floor before freezing a clone target

A fresh pass took its target from the source's watermark at the moment it
started. This node's own capture picks its first block much later, once sync
leaves it state to walk, and the chain moves in between - so the target landed
below the capture start and the two ranges could not touch. Nothing could
publish, and the only repair the protocol has for a gap is re-streaming every
column from scratch, which discarded hours of finished work and then set up to
do it again.

The floor is now required before a source is chosen, so the target is picked to
reach it and the gap never opens. This costs the wait for capture to start once,
which is time already being lost to the discarded pass.

Resumed passes are unaffected: they carry a frozen target and must continue
against it.

* fix(network): stop punishing a static peer for a disconnect this node chose

Reconnection delays exist so a discovery-fed pool stops hammering peers that
keep failing. A static peer is not discovered - it is named by the operator -
and the commonest reason its stats carry a recent disconnect is that this node
hung up on it deliberately. Backing off then left the only clone source
unreachable for minutes after every hangup, which was most of the lost time. The
five-second dial debounce already bounds the retry rate.

A wedged session is also detected sooner: the serving node answers every scan
well inside its deadline, so two consecutive thirty-second silences mean the
session is stuck rather than busy, and waiting for five spent two and a half
minutes proving what two prove.

The slow-serve log now reports at three seconds instead of twenty, with the
entry count, so the next run shows whether responses are slow to build or fast
to build and lost afterwards.

* diag(nhist): trace a rows request from send to answer

Nothing in the logs distinguishes a request that never reached the serving node
from one it answered into a dead socket, so every diagnosis of the clone stalls
has been a guess. The serving side now reports each rows request as it arrives
and again as it is answered, with the entry count and how long the scan took,
and the requesting side reports the ones it gives up on with the same column,
start key and cursor.

Matching the two logs across a stall separates three causes that need three
different fixes: the request never arrived, it arrived and went unanswered, or
it was answered and the reply never landed.

* diag(nhist): move the per-request rows trace behind debug

A serving node answers several rows requests a second, so tracing each one at
info buried every other line in its log. The trace stays, at debug, where it can
be turned on for the minutes it takes to diagnose a stall and left off the rest
of the time.

Both lines now print the whole key rather than its first eight bytes. A history
row key is the flat key followed by the block, so a truncated cursor looks
identical across every version of the same account - which reads exactly like a
cursor that never advances, and cost an afternoon of chasing a livelock that was
not there.

What stays at info is what only appears when something is wrong: a scan past
three seconds, and a request the requester gave up on.

* fix(network): stop a stale dial flag from stranding a static peer

A static peer whose IsAwaitingConnection stayed set was skipped by the dial loop
forever, and the skip only logged at debug, so a node that lost its one clone
source sat idle for five hours without a single line saying why. The flag is now
trusted only for as long as a dial could plausibly still be running; past that
the peer is dialed again and the reason is reported at info.

Consecutive row timeouts go back to five. Cutting them to two found a wedged
session a minute sooner but tripled the number of disconnects, and every one of
those was another chance to hit the stranding above - trading ninety seconds of
detection for hours of silence is a bad bargain, and the recovery path has to be
trustworthy before the detection is made twitchier.

* test(flat-history): pin that a height's accounts reproduce its state root

Before spending a resync on widening the account key, this pins the half of the
claim that can be checked today: what history returns at a height - nonce,
balance, storage root, code hash - is correct and complete enough to rebuild
that height's root exactly.

It reads accounts by address, which a test can do and a scan cannot, so it
deliberately does not cover enumeration. That is the part the truncated key
blocks, and turning this test into the regression for it means only changing how
the accounts are found, not what is done with them.

* test(flat-history): red until an account row carries its whole trie path

Deliberately failing: an account history row keys by the first 20 bytes of the
path, so a scan of the column cannot place a leaf and no root can be rebuilt
from history a node was handed. Expected 32, was 20.

The rest of the test already passes and is what makes the failure worth acting
on: the values history returns at a height rebuild that height's root exactly,
so addressing is the only thing missing, not the data.

Goes green when the history account key widens to the full path.

* fix(flat-history): guard the 20/32-byte key boundary the account-key widening opened

A six-reviewer pass on the account-key widening (20 -> 32 bytes) found several
places where a wide key could still be silently mishandled as narrow: scope
resolution could fall back to the general floor instead of refusing, and the
archive-clone importer accepted a wrong-width row with no check at all. It also
found the clone-serving byte budget charging the raw key length instead of the
wire's delta-encoded length, and a drain in HistoryScopeGate that could forget
about a reader admitted during a timed-out drain attempt. This closes those
gaps and cleans up the stale comments, dead code, and magic numbers the review
also turned up, without changing any wire-visible behavior.

* feat(flat-history): prove an archive against its own headers at every block

The sampled marker check inside the clone pass stays the fast publish gate;
this is the definitive content proof behind it. Starting from the state the
rows alone produce at a range's start - anchored to that block's header before
anything walks - it applies each block's recorded post-values forward and
compares the recomputed root to every block's header, so a change attributed
to the wrong block is caught at exactly the height whose as-of answers it
would poison, which the tip root can never show. Storage tries are rebuilt
and checked against each account record's own storageRoot whenever its slots
change, and the captured per-block marker is compared to the header too,
since serving trusts the marker rather than anything rebuilt. No execution
is involved: headers already are consensus-verified execution output, so the
only open question is whether these rows reproduce those commitments.

Ranges are independently anchored at both ends and share nothing but the
read-only columns, so the walk parallelizes by splitting the chain. v2 only:
its rows are the walk's instructions verbatim, while a windowed database
stores pre-values, keeps no rows for unchanged keys, and has pruned the
ancestry a genesis-anchored walk needs - asking for it fails at startup.

Off by default behind Flat.HistoryVerifyEveryBlock. A verified range's
working set is held in memory for now, so a full mainnet archive should wait
for the spill-store hardening before enabling.

* refactor(flat-history): drop the p2p clone, sidecar and serving program

Remove the nhist/1 subprotocol, archive clone streaming, peer-fed window
import, changeset sidecar and history serving end to end: protocol handler,
messages, ENR advertisement, peer selection and serving slots, coordinators,
steps, config flags, metrics, rocksdb options and their tests. The branch
keeps only the 32-byte account path, the rolling retention window with its
pruner, the per-contract slices and the every-block walk verifier.

The ChangesetSidecar column family entry stays so existing databases that
already created it keep opening; nothing reads or writes it anymore.
ICloneHeaderSource becomes IHistoryHeaderSource - it is the verifier's
header seam now, not a clone concern. StartHistoryWalkVerification joins
the optional steps of BuildInSteps_IsCorrect, missed when the step was
introduced.

* fix(flat-history): review-pass fixes, dead-seam removal and doc trims

Correctness and concurrency fixes from the six-reviewer pass:
- HistoryScopeGate: floor-generation registry replaces the two-epoch
  counter - a timed-out drain no longer strands the census new scopes keep
  joining, so retries wait only on scopes admitted under an older floor
  and window pruning can never silently stop for the process lifetime.
- A slice retention shallower than HistoryRetentionBlocks is refused at
  reconcile: it would delete that address's rows inside the general
  window while reads still resolve them from live state.
- The restricted reader folds into HistoryBackedPersistenceReader and
  resolves its slice scope set after EnterScope, closing the race where a
  concurrent floor advance invalidated a pre-entry snapshot.
- Bundle construction disposes the reader on a later throw instead of
  leaking its scope; the pruner commits deletes before persisting the
  resume cursor; wake-signal and Parallel.For shutdown races fixed.

Capture-path and scan costs: PendingV3Writes is reused across rounds
instead of rebuilt per block, the pending map updates in one lookup,
ResolvePendingV3 reads the persisted column in key order, the format key
stamps once per process instead of per block, and the pruner and walk
verifier scans pass HintCacheMiss so they stop evicting the live working
set from the shared block cache.

Seams orphaned by the p2p strip removed end to end: INodeRecordContributor
and the provider hook, CompactRange and the column Tune, the protocol
timeout parameters, PeerManager's unused sync-config dependency (whose
stale test call site had broken the discovery test project's build),
HistoryAvailability's subscriber-less event, the pivot seeder's unused
reader parameter and HistoryKeyLayout's identity-copy encoder. The slice
address list now has one parser, shared by state retention and receipt
retention. The one-fixture Init.Test project folds into Runner.Test.

New regression tests cover the v3 in-walk pre-value chaining, the
shallow-slice refusal, bounded slice floors advancing with the watermark,
the publish-then-defer-deletes drain contract, windowing-vs-v2 refusal
and the restricted routing arm. Test narration comments and oversized doc
essays trimmed throughout.

* refactor(flat-history): simpler shape, zero-alloc capture, complete slice receipts

The window keeps flatHistory to its four columns and nothing else: the
retired ChangesetSidecar column family name goes too, so a fresh database
creates exactly AccountHistory, StorageHistory, AvailableBlocks and
StorageClears. Databases created by earlier builds need a flatHistory
wipe, which the fresh genesis syncs already imply.

Capture no longer allocates per touch: the pending pre-value maps key on
value structs (account path, and account path + slot hash), and the flat
key bytes are re-encoded into a caller buffer only when a pending row is
actually written. Resolution still walks the persisted column in sorted
order.

The walk verifier scans each history column once and routes rows to the
owning segment, so segment count multiplies concurrency instead of IO -
previously every segment re-scanned all three columns end to end.

Retained slice receipts now serve completely: a by-hash receipt read for
a block whose body was pruned falls back to the header and decodes the
self-describing record standalone; on legacy-keyed databases the retain
deletes the plain-hash entry that would shadow it with the undecodable
compact copy; and the retain sweep no longer pollutes the live receipts
LRU. TryRetainSelfDescribing becomes a default interface member instead
of a marker-interface downcast.

The pruner and the walk-verification coordinator start from their steps
via explicit Start() instead of constructor side effects, the coordinator
moves next to the verifier in State.Flat.History and its fixture follows,
and the slice parser lives once in Nethermind.Db. Quality sweep: dead
satellite-protocol extension removed, trace levels restored, one type per
file, span idioms, scope list held as an array on the restricted read
path.

* fix(flat-history): address PR review and clear the code-style gate

Close the v3 read-order race by reading the live column before seeking
history, so a capture round completing between the two reads is still
caught. Refuse a SeedPivot below an already published floor instead of
silently lowering it. Report the destruct enumeration-cap poison through
a counter and a warn log naming the account and block. Count a walk
segment's anchor block once so BlocksCompared stays exact. Restore the
snap-serving decider modules to their master versions - that flip is a
separate networking decision and it broke the flat E2E sync test.

Turn the address parser's empty catch into a FormatException guard,
which is the exception Address.TryParse actually lets through, and set
the floor metric where the floor is published. Remove unused usings
across the branch so EnforceCodeStyleInBuild reports no IDE or CA
warnings.

* fix(flat-history): close the remaining PR review findings

Splice a storage-wiping destruct into the chain of slots first written
lower in the same capture walk. The destruct only enumerates persisted
slots, so a slot written at an earlier block of the walk got no
pre-value row and every read between the two blocks fell through to
live state the destruct had already cleared.

Ask RocksDB for total-order seek only where a range view can leave the
prefix bucket its seek lands in, measured against the widest extractor
configured for the database, instead of on every range view in the
process. Give the reader's view the same treatment plus the read-ahead
hint it was dropping.

Move the window pruner onto its own thread - a pass is synchronous for
seconds and the scope drain blocks - and make a yielded pass wait as
long as it just ran, so a backlog cannot become an uninterrupted
scan-and-delete. Remember the deletes owed when a drain times out, so
the next pass resumes them rather than seeing no floor advance.

Refuse a walk verification whose partition would not fit in memory,
naming the limit and the way out, and stop carrying clears from above
the range. Its footprint follows state size, not range length, so
chunking cannot help and the docs now say so.

Give the history pruner an injected receipt-retention policy that never
retains by default, bound only where slices are configured, so the
generic pruner no longer takes flat-db config or the log index and no
longer knows what a slice is.

* revert(network): drop the static-peer and satellite-protocol changes

None of it serves what is left on this branch. The static-peer redial
path existed for the clone feeder and consumer, which are gone, and the
session-keyed satellite registration existed for the nhist subprotocol,
which is gone with them - including the deletion of a public extension
method that out-of-tree plugins can still be calling.

Peering behaviour belongs in front of the sync and network owners on its
own, not carried along by a history feature, so these six files go back
to master untouched.

* fix(flat-history): repair two regressions the review pass introduced

Registering the never-retain default plainly in BlockTreeModule meant it
won: that module loads after the flat-history one and Autofac keeps the
last registration, so a node with slices configured silently resolved
the default and dropped its sliced addresses' receipts at the expiry
boundary. The default now preserves any existing one, and a container
test over the real module graph asserts which policy a sliced node gets
- the only kind of test that can see an ordering bug at all.

Deferring the owed deletes after a drain timeout skipped the drain on
the way back in, and that path is precisely the one whose readers are
still open, so the next pass deleted rows a live historical scope was
resolving through and it answered from tip state instead of failing
closed. The gate now separates bumping the generation from waiting on
it, so a retry waits for exactly the scopes that were open when the
floor was published - re-bumping would also demote every reader
admitted since, which are safe and must not hold the pruner up.

Also: a v3 read no longer pays a live lookup on a hit, since a found row
is always the answer; the miss path seeks again after the live read to
settle a round that committed in between. Make both Dispose paths
idempotent, keep the mutable scope array inside the assembly, read
prefix_extractor=nullptr as no extractor rather than the widest one, and
drop the LINQ from the address parse.

* feat(db): let a store drop a whole key range in one operation

Adds IRangeRemovableKeyValueStore alongside the other capability
interfaces, implemented over RocksDB's range tombstone and mirrored in
MemDb so callers can be tested without a real database. The cost does
not scale with how many keys the range holds, which only pays off where
the keys are ordered along the dimension being dropped - the block
stores are, being keyed by number then hash.

The tombstone goes through a write batch rather than the database
directly, so it reaches the WAL and a crash cannot resurrect a range its
owner has already stopped serving.

Nothing calls this yet.

The tests pin the bounds, which is the whole safety story: the lower one
inclusive, the upper one exclusive, neighbours on both sides untouched,
an empty range a no-op, the tombstone surviving a reopen, and every hash
at every covered height going - including the ones no level record
lists, which a per-block loop leaves behind forever.

* fix(history): publish the pruning boundary before reclaiming behind it

Pruning could not finish. Each pass read two full block bodies and wrote
one tombstone per transaction, so clearing a 19M-block backlog meant
reading roughly as much as it freed - and observed passes managed one to
five blocks each, which does not terminate, it merely runs forever.

The boundary a pruning node announces is now a policy decision rather
than an outcome of disk throughput: it moves to the cutoff in one
metadata write, and the disk is given back behind it in bounded steps.
Removing a range costs the same whatever it spans, so a step is a
handful of operations reading nothing at all.

Splitting the announced boundary from a reclaim cursor is what makes an
interrupted pass safe. The boundary can never be starved, and everything
the reclaim touches has already been declared absent - so a reclaim that
is slow, cancelled or lost to a crash leaves the node honest and merely
fat, resuming from the persisted cursor. The gate and the resume point
both read that cursor, not the boundary; they part company the moment a
pass is cut short, and only the cursor knows where the disk stands.

The transaction index is deliberately left alone. Enumerating it is what
forced the body read per block, and its entries are an accelerator, not
the record: one resolving to a block that is gone already answer…</pre>

description:
fix(xdc): resolve epochs below the fast sync pivot without their snapshots (#12974)

* fix(xdc): resolve epochs below the fast sync pivot for penalty lookback

After a fast sync the node logged "Cannot recover snapshot for block N:
block not processed" on repeat, one epoch below the oldest gap block
state sync had prepared. Two causes, both fixed here.

XdcStateSyncSnapshotManager.GetGapBlocks prepared gap snapshots only from
the pivot's own epoch switch forward, but the penalty comeback check at an
epoch switch reads the penalties of the previous LimitPenaltyEpoch epoch
switch blocks. Gap blocks now reach that far back, floored at the switch
block so the existing V1 branch and near-genesis cases are unchanged.

Reaching an older epoch also went through GetEpochSwitchInfo, which returns
null without that epoch's snapshot even though navigation only needs the
epoch switch block itself. FindEpochSwitchBlock walks headers alone, and
GetBlockByEpochNumber uses it (in both the mainnet and subnet managers)
along with a snapshot free between-walk. GetEpochSwitchInfo keeps its
contract, so callers that want the master node set still get a hard null.

When the lookback failed, no penalized node ever accumulated the epochs
needed for parole, so every one of them was re-penalized and the epoch
switch block would be rejected with "Penalties does not match".

LimitPenaltyEpoch and LimitPenaltyEpochV2 move from the chainspec and
release spec to XdcConstants at 4 and 0, matching the reference client.
This changes the testnet parole window from 5 to 4; mainnet never set
either value and stays on the V2 branch, so it is unaffected.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 

* fix(xdc): wait for the headers state sync needs instead of failing on them

Addresses the PR review.

GetGapBlocks now returns null when any header it needs is missing rather
than casting a null header into the target queue, and XdcStateSyncPivot
treats that as "not ready" instead of latching an incomplete queue for the
rest of the run. The header sync downloads the pivot itself
(HeadersSyncFeed.ResetPivot requests pivot + 1 downwards), so neither the
pivot nor its gap blocks exist when state sync first polls; TreeSync
already handles a null pivot header by falling asleep and retrying. This
also makes it possible to drop Sync.NeedToWaitForHeader, which currently
blocks state and full sync until every header down to the barrier is in.

Floor the penalty lookback on the switch block's epoch base rather than the
switch block itself, so an unaligned SwitchBlock cannot put the first gap
block off the epoch grid.

FindEpochSwitchHeader replaces FindEpochSwitchBlock: it returns the header,
so the between-walk no longer re-reads it, caches the resolved epoch switch
per queried header, and reports null for pre-switch blocks that carry no
round, matching what GetEpochSwitchInfo did. GetEpochSwitchInfoBetween is
now expressed in terms of that walk, so there is one traversal to reason
about, and an epoch the walk only passes through no longer needs its
snapshot.

Cite the reference client for the two penalty constants.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 

* fix(xdc): drop the gap block lookback, header-only navigation covers it

The penalty comeback loop calls GetEpochSwitchInfo with the same hash on
every iteration — the parent of the epoch switch block — so the only
snapshot it needs is the current epoch's, which GetGapBlocks already
prepared. The older epochs it reaches through GetBlockByEpochNumber, which
no longer touches a snapshot, and reads as header.PenaltiesAddress.

So widening the gap block window was treating the symptom: the defect was
that epoch navigation demanded snapshots it did not need. Reverting it also
removes the lookback floor, LimitPenaltyEpoch as an input to state sync, and
five extra state roots per sync.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 

* docs(xdc): drop the moved penalty constants from the README, log pivot waits

Three points from the re-review.

The README still documented LimitPenaltyEpoch and LimitPenaltyEpochV2 as
chainspec parameters. Unknown members are skipped on load, so an out-of-tree
subnet chainspec carrying the key would load clean and silently run at the
constant.

FindEpochSwitchHeader only consulted the cache for the queried header, so a
new head re-walked the whole epoch where GetEpochSwitchInfo costs one step.
The parent's entry is valid for the child exactly when the child is not
itself an epoch switch, which the loop has already established.

XdcStateSyncPivot returned without a word when it could not initialize, and
StateSyncRunner only logs that at Debug, so a pivot that never resolves was
silent at default log level. It now reports the first wait and the eventual
readiness at Info, which is what a NeedToWaitForHeader soak test would need.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 

* fix(xdc): keep LimitPenaltyEpoch in the chainspec, it is consensus critical

Syncing Apothem rejected block 85542743 with "Validators does not match
what's stored in snapshot minus its penalty". That block is an epoch switch,
and the validator set it is compared against is candidates minus penalties,
so a penalty set that differs by one address surfaces as a validator
mismatch. Moving LimitPenaltyEpoch to a constant took the window from the 5
the testnet chainspec carries to 4, and a smaller window paroles strictly
more nodes: any node penalised in exactly the last 4 epochs with enough
signing transactions came back for us and stayed penalised on chain.

So the value is per network after all. Restore it on V2ConfigParams and the
release spec, restore Apothem's 5, and pin what both chain specs resolve to
so losing the value again fails a test rather than a sync.

LimitPenaltyEpochV2 stays a constant, since no chainspec ever set it, and
becomes 1 with the +1 dropped from the comeback height. The pre-upgrade
branch reads a single epoch of penalties, which the lookback argument now
states outright instead of spelling it as a window size of zero.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 

* style(xdc): drop usings left unused by this branch

Both fail the code-lint job, which treats any IDE or CA warning as an error.
Nethermind.Core.Crypto went unused in EpochSwitchManager when the between
walk stopped tracking an iterator hash, and System in XdcStateSyncPivot when
the missing pivot header stopped throwing.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 

* test(xdc): cover the rewritten epoch switch walk on the mainnet manager

GetEpochSwitchInfoBetween was restructured into a header-only walk plus a
resolve pass with nothing pinning it: the subnet tests exercise an override,
and the only production callers mock the manager.

Four cases, modelled on the subnet ones. The one that matters is an epoch
the walk passes through below the requested range having no snapshot, which
now succeeds; checked out against master's implementation it fails with
"Expected: not null, But was: null". The rest pin equivalence.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 

* Update src/Nethermind/Nethermind.Xdc/PenaltyHandler.cs

* Update src/Nethermind/Nethermind.Xdc/EpochSwitchManager.cs

* Update src/Nethermind/Nethermind.Xdc/BaseEpochSwitchManager.cs

* Update src/Nethermind/Nethermind.Xdc/XdcConstants.cs

* refactor(xdc): step into the previous epoch by hash, report each pivot wait

Two points from the re-review.

GetEpochSwitchBlocksBetween resolved the quorum certificate target before
re-checking the loop condition, so a walk that already had everything it
needed returned null when that header was missing — one below the header
barrier, say. Carrying the iterator as a hash and resolving it at the top
restores what master did through GetEpochSwitchInfo(Hash256).

The pivot latched on having logged rather than on the reason, and since the
pivot header resolves before its gap blocks, the first message was almost
always the pivot one and stuck there. Those two states are the whole point
of the message, so latch on the reason instead.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5

Release v1.14.1

Bundles

  • Fix bundle deploy failing with deployment_source.source_code_path cannot be set on UpdateApp (400) when updating an app that has an active deployment (#6401).
  • Fixed ${resources...} references to resource keys starting with an underscore (e.g. _my_job). On the direct engine, deploying such a resource with permissions or grants failed with cannot parse "/jobs/${resources.jobs._my_job.id}", and user-written references to it were silently left unresolved (#6422)

Notable Changes

  • Bundles still on Terraform state are now migrated to the direct engine automatically, after a deploy whose dry-run conversion comes back clean. To opt out, set engine: terraform under bundle or DATABRICKS_BUNDLE_ENGINE=terraform. See https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/dev-tools/bundles/direct

CLI

  • Fixed idle databricks ssh connect sessions disconnecting after a few minutes, on dedicated clusters and on serverless. The tunnel now keeps itself warm: the SSH client and the SSH server on the compute exchange keepalives every 30 seconds, and the CLI's proxy pings the tunnel's websocket every 20 seconds. A session nobody is typing into stays connected, with no need to set ServerAliveInterval by hand.

Bundles

  • bundle plan no longer reports a permanent, unconvergeable update on securable_kind for Unity Catalog TABLE securables declared under an app's resources. The field is computed by the backend (output-only), so it is now ignored during drift detection. Direct engine only (#6342).
  • Add support for the cluster_policies resource type in Declarative Automation Bundles. Cluster policies are only supported in direct deployment mode.
  • bundle destroy no longer counts resources that are already gone remotely in its Destroy: N deleted summary. Such deletes only clean up stale state and are not listed under the deletion prompt, so they are now excluded from the count as well, matching the terraform engine.
  • bundle destroy now also removes the directory named after the bundle, not just the target directory beneath it, when workspace.root_path ends in ${bundle.name}/${bundle.target} — which includes the default root path. It is removed non-recursively, so it stays in place while another target of the same bundle is still deployed there. Previously every destroy left an empty directory behind (#6317).
  • job_runs now plans skip for a run that is still in progress and when on_bundle_deploy is removed, instead of treating either case as an update. (#6357)
  • Added DATABRICKS_BUNDLE_RESOURCE_MAX_WAIT (in seconds) to cap how long deploy and destroy wait for a resource. Direct engine only.
  • Fixed bundle deploy on the direct engine failing with Nothing to update, or reporting a change it never applied, when a schema, catalog, volume, registered model or external location field was removed from the configuration or set outside the bundle. The update now sends the fields the plan reports as cleared instead of dropping them.

Dependency Updates

  • Bump github.com/databricks/databricks-sdk-go from v0.171.0 to v0.175.0 (#6322).
  • Bump Terraform provider from v1.127.0 to v1.128.0 (#6323).

description:
PyDABs codegen: load types by reachability instead of a manual namespace allowlist (#6393)

## Changes

PyDABs codegen previously loaded types from a hand-maintained
`LOADED_NAMESPACES` allowlist in `packages.py`. Adding a resource whose
fields reference a new namespace required editing that list — and
because the list was applied *before* the generator's dependency walk, a
missing namespace surfaced as a `KeyError` deep in generation, forcing
an add-namespace-and-rerun loop.

This replaces the allowlist with reachability: `get_schemas()` now walks
`$ref`s from the root resource types (`RESOURCE_TYPES`) and loads
exactly their transitive closure.

- Remove `LOADED_NAMESPACES` and `should_load_ref` from `packages.py`.
- Add `_collect_reachable_refs` / `_refs_in_raw_schema` to
`jsonschema.py`; the reachable set is used only as a membership filter
while iterating `flat_spec` in its original order.

## Why

- The generator already prunes to each resource's reachable closure
(`_collect_reachable_schemas`), so the allowlist duplicated that logic
in a coarser, manual form.
- Loading the closure is also what avoids the handful of spec types the
parser can't model (e.g. `variable.*`): they aren't reachable from any
resource, so they're never loaded — no allowlist needed to dodge them.
- A type genuinely reachable from a resource that fails to parse still
raises a clear `Failed to parse schema for `, instead of a later
`KeyError`.

## Tests

- Regenerating (`pydabs-codegen`) produces byte-identical output under
`python/databricks/bundles/` — the change is behavior-preserving for the
currently supported resources.
- `codegen_tests` (8) and PyDABs unit tests (211) pass; edited files
pass ruff format + lint.

Note: iterating the reachable set directly reordered schema parsing and
produced import-wrapping churn in the generated files (ruff formats
imports differently by input order). Filtering `flat_spec` in its
original order keeps regeneration a clean no-op.
